Start with a six-block backbone. Then build it again and add five side chains,
the comb's “hairs”. Finally, put the same eleven blocks into a single linear
chain to see what branching changes.

This tutorial builds on [Diblock copolymer](diblock-copolymer.qmd) and
[What is a reference point?](reference-points.qmd). Lengths are in nm and q is
in inverse nm.

## 1. Build and view the backbone

Use one `Add` followed by five `Link` calls. Each link adds the next block
at the preceding block's endpoint:

```text
b1 -- b2 -- b3 -- b4 -- b5 -- b6
```

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pyseb

parameters = {
    "beta_backbone": 1.0,
    "Rg_backbone": 2.0,
    "beta_side": 0.8,
    "Rg_side": 3.0,
}

backbone = pyseb.World("BackboneTutorial")
graph = backbone.Add("GaussianPolymer", "b1", "backbone")
backbone.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b2.end1", "b1.end2", "backbone")
backbone.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b3.end1", "b2.end2", "backbone")
backbone.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b4.end1", "b3.end2", "backbone")
backbone.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b5.end1", "b4.end2", "backbone")
backbone.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b6.end1", "b5.end2", "backbone")
backbone.Add(graph, "molecule")

backbone_view = pyseb.visualize(backbone, "molecule", parameters, height=400)
```

The names `b1` to `b6` identify individual blocks. Their shared `backbone`
tag means they all use `Rg_backbone` and `beta_backbone`. The `side`
parameters will be used when we add the hairs below.

## 2. Build the backbone again, then add hairs

Repeat those six blocks in a new world. This time, attach a side chain at
each of the five internal backbone junctions:

```text
b1 --+-- b2 --+-- b3 --+-- b4 --+-- b5 --+-- b6
     |       |       |       |       |
     s1      s2      s3      s4      s5
```

```{python}
comb = pyseb.World("CombTutorial")
graph = comb.Add("GaussianPolymer", "b1", "backbone")
comb.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b2.end1", "b1.end2", "backbone")
comb.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b3.end1", "b2.end2", "backbone")
comb.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b4.end1", "b3.end2", "backbone")
comb.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b5.end1", "b4.end2", "backbone")
comb.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b6.end1", "b5.end2", "backbone")

comb.Link("GaussianPolymer", "s1.end1", "b1.end2", "side")
comb.Link("GaussianPolymer", "s2.end1", "b2.end2", "side")
comb.Link("GaussianPolymer", "s3.end1", "b3.end2", "side")
comb.Link("GaussianPolymer", "s4.end1", "b4.end2", "side")
comb.Link("GaussianPolymer", "s5.end1", "b5.end2", "side")
comb.Add(graph, "molecule")

comb_view = pyseb.visualize(comb, "molecule", parameters, height=440)
```

The five extra `Link` calls are the only change in construction. For example,
`b1.end2`, `b2.end1`, and `s1.end1` now meet at the same junction. Each hair
uses the shared `side` parameters.

These are fixed endpoint junctions, rather than attachments sampled along
a polymer contour. The blocks can change conformation and rotate relative
to each other; the junction does not impose a fixed angle.

## 3. Put the same eleven blocks into a linear chain

Adding hairs changed both composition and connectivity relative to the bare
backbone. To isolate **connectivity**, keep all eleven blocks and connect
`s1` through `s5` end to end after `b6`:

```text
b1 -- b2 -- b3 -- b4 -- b5 -- b6 -- s1 -- s2 -- s3 -- s4 -- s5
```

```{python}
linear = pyseb.World("LinearTutorial")
graph = linear.Add("GaussianPolymer", "b1", "backbone")
linear.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b2.end1", "b1.end2", "backbone")
linear.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b3.end1", "b2.end2", "backbone")
linear.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b4.end1", "b3.end2", "backbone")
linear.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b5.end1", "b4.end2", "backbone")
linear.Link("GaussianPolymer", "b6.end1", "b5.end2", "backbone")

linear.Link("GaussianPolymer", "s1.end1", "b6.end2", "side")
linear.Link("GaussianPolymer", "s2.end1", "s1.end2", "side")
linear.Link("GaussianPolymer", "s3.end1", "s2.end2", "side")
linear.Link("GaussianPolymer", "s4.end1", "s3.end2", "side")
linear.Link("GaussianPolymer", "s5.end1", "s4.end2", "side")
linear.Add(graph, "molecule")

linear_view = pyseb.visualize(linear, "molecule", parameters, height=440)
```

The comb and this linear chain use identical block dimensions, scattering
weights, and total composition. Only the attachment references differ.

All three viewers show representative random walks. Their precise shapes
are not the scattering calculation: SEB averages over conformations.
Crossings in a picture do not create links, and these ideal Gaussian blocks
have no excluded-volume interactions.

## 4. Compare the comb and the eleven-block chain

```{python}
q = np.geomspace(1e-3, 2.0, 180)

comb_rg2 = comb.EvaluateRadiusOfGyration2("molecule", parameters)
linear_rg2 = linear.EvaluateRadiusOfGyration2("molecule", parameters)
print(f"Comb: Rg = {np.sqrt(comb_rg2):.4f} nm")
print(f"Linear chain: Rg = {np.sqrt(linear_rg2):.4f} nm")

comb_curve = comb.EvaluateFormFactor("molecule", parameters, q.tolist())
linear_curve = linear.EvaluateFormFactor("molecule", parameters, q.tolist())

plt.loglog(q, comb_curve, label="Comb: six backbone blocks + five hairs")
plt.loglog(q, linear_curve, label="Linear: the same eleven blocks")
plt.xlabel(r"$q$ (nm$^{-1}$)")
plt.ylabel(r"$F(q)$")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

Both normalized curves start at one. Branching shortens the paths between
blocks, making this comb more compact than the eleven-block linear chain.
Their different radii of gyration therefore already distinguish them at
small q. Unlike the [rod–coil comparison](rod-coil.qmd), we hold composition
and block dimensions fixed rather than matching overall size.

## 5. Hide the hairs by contrast matching

Set `beta_side` to zero. The hairs remain in the comb, but contribute no
scattering. The same applies to the five terminal side-type blocks in the
linear model. Both curves now reproduce the original six-block backbone:

```{python}
matched = dict(parameters, beta_side=0.0)
comb_matched = comb.EvaluateFormFactor("molecule", matched, q.tolist())
linear_matched = linear.EvaluateFormFactor("molecule", matched, q.tolist())
backbone_curve = backbone.EvaluateFormFactor("molecule", parameters, q.tolist())

np.testing.assert_allclose(comb_matched, backbone_curve, rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12)
np.testing.assert_allclose(linear_matched, backbone_curve, rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12)

plt.loglog(q, backbone_curve, label="Original backbone")
plt.loglog(q, comb_matched, "--", label="Comb: hairs contrast matched")
plt.loglog(q, linear_matched, ":", label="Linear: side-type blocks contrast matched")
plt.xlabel(r"$q$ (nm$^{-1}$)")
plt.ylabel(r"$F(q)$")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

The overlap shows that branching invisible, non-interacting chains onto the
backbone does not change its scattering in this model.

Try changing `Rg_side` with both families visible. Then vary the side-chain
scattering weight separately. Changing a dimension and changing contrast
answer different questions, even though either can change the measured curve.
